claim: VHL inactivation is a primary event in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).
source: Whereas VHL inactivation is a primary event in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), the precise mechanism(s) of how this interacts with the secondary mutations in tumor suppressor genes, including PBRM1, KDM5C/JARID1C, SETD2, and/or BAP1, remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: VHL, PBRM1, and KDM5C share a common regulation of interferon response expression signature.
source: Gene expression analyses reveal that VHL, PBRM1, or KDM5C share a common regulation of interferon response expression signature.
evidence: Supported by gene expression analyses described in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of HIF2α, PBRM1, or KDM5C in VHL-/- cells reduces the expression of interferon stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3).
source: Loss of HIF2α, PBRM1, or KDM5C in VHL-/-cells reduces the expression of interferon stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3), a transcription factor that regulates the interferon signature.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: ISGF3 is a transcription factor that regulates the interferon signature.
source: Loss of HIF2α, PBRM1, or KDM5C in VHL-/-cells reduces the expression of interferon stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3), a transcription factor that regulates the interferon signature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ISGF3 function.

claim: Loss of SETD2 or BAP1 reduces the ISGF3 level.
source: Moreover, loss of SETD2 or BAP1 also reduces the ISGF3 level.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ISGF3 is strongly tumor-suppressive in a xenograft model.
source: Finally, ISGF3 is strongly tumor-suppressive in a xenograft model as its loss significantly enhances tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of ISGF3 significantly enhances tumor growth.
source: Finally, ISGF3 is strongly tumor-suppressive in a xenograft model as its loss significantly enhances tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reactivation of ISGF3 retards tumor growth by PBRM1-deficient ccRCC cells.
source: Conversely, reactivation of ISGF3 retards tumor growth by PBRM1-deficient ccRCC cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing tumor growth inhibition upon ISGF3 overexpression.

claim: HIF induces ISGF3 after VHL inactivation.
source: Thus after VHL inactivation, HIF induces ISGF3, which is reversed by the loss of secondary tumor suppressors, suggesting that this is a key negative feedback loop in ccRCC.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that HIF2α loss reduces ISGF3 levels.

claim: Loss of secondary tumor suppressors reverses HIF-induced ISGF3.
source: Thus after VHL inactivation, HIF induces ISGF3, which is reversed by the loss of secondary tumor suppressors, suggesting that this is a key negative feedback loop in ccRCC.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that loss of PBRM1, KDM5C, SETD2, or BAP1 reduces ISGF3 levels.

claim: The HIF-ISGF3 pathway represents a key negative feedback loop in ccRCC.
source: Thus after VHL inactivation, HIF induces ISGF3, which is reversed by the loss of secondary tumor suppressors, suggesting that this is a key negative feedback loop in ccRCC.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Kidney cancer is among the top ten cancers in both incidence and mortality in both men and women.
source: Kidney cancer is among the top ten cancers, both in incidence and mortality in both men and women.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Approximately 70-80% of ccRCC are sporadic tumors that harbor biallelic inactivation of VHL.
source: Approximately 70 – 80% of ccRCC are sporadic tumors that harbor biallelic inactivation of VHL (Linehan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Germline VHL mutation leads to early-onset bilateral kidney tumors in hereditary kidney cancer.
source: In the rare disease of hereditary kidney cancer, germline VHL mutation leads to early-onset bilateral kidney tumors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VHL-associated hereditary kidney cancer.

claim: pVHL acts as the substrate recognition module of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex.
source: Biochemically, the protein product of the VHL tumor suppressor gene pVHL acts as the substrate recognition module of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about pVHL function.

claim: The pVHL E3 ubiquitin ligase complex targets HIFα subunits for poly-ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation.
source: This complex targets the α subunits of the heterodimeric transcription factor Hypoxia-Inducible Factor (HIF) for poly-ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation (Zhang and Yang, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HIFα is hydroxylated on either of two prolyl residues by members of the EglN family under normal oxygen tension.
source: When HIFα is hydroxylated on either of two prolyl residues by members of the EglN family (also called PHDs or HPHs) under normal oxygen tension, it is recognized by pVHL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIFα regulation.

claim: Hydroxylated HIFα is recognized by pVHL.
source: When HIFα is hydroxylated on either of two prolyl residues by members of the EglN family (also called PHDs or HPHs) under normal oxygen tension, it is recognized by pVHL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIFα-pVHL interaction.

claim: Without pVHL, HIFα protein accumulates and activates the hypoxia response transcriptional program.
source: Without pVHL, HIFα protein accumulates and activates the hypoxia response transcriptional program.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the consequence of VHL loss.

claim: Constitutively active HIF drives ccRCC tumorigenesis and tumor growth.
source: This constitutively active HIF subsequently drives ccRCC tumorigenesis and tumor growth (Kaelin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HIF targets include both tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressive genes.
source: Interestingly, HIF targets include both tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressive genes, but its overall activity is potently oncogenic (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The overall activity of HIF is potently oncogenic.
source: Interestingly, HIF targets include both tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressive genes, but its overall activity is potently oncogenic (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Restoration of pVHL in VHL-/- ccRCC cells suppresses their ability to form tumors in immune-compromised mice.
source: Restoration of pVHL in VHL-/- ccRCC cells suppresses their ability to form tumors in immune-compromised mice, while stabilization of HIF2α overrides the effect of pVHL (Kondo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Stabilization of HIF2α overrides the tumor-suppressive effect of pVHL.
source: Restoration of pVHL in VHL-/- ccRCC cells suppresses their ability to form tumors in immune-compromised mice, while stabilization of HIF2α overrides the effect of pVHL (Kondo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HIF2α suppression in VHL-/- ccRCC cells cripples their ability to form tumors.
source: Conversely, HIF2α suppression in VHL-/- ccRCC cells cripples their ability to form tumors (Zimmer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The current standard of care for metastatic ccRCC focuses on inhibiting the VEGF receptor.
source: The current standard of care for metastatic ccRCC focuses on inhibiting the VEGF receptor, yet drug resistance eventually develops in most cases.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Drug resistance eventually develops in most cases of metastatic ccRCC treated with VEGF receptor inhibitors.
source: The current standard of care for metastatic ccRCC focuses on inhibiting the VEGF receptor, yet drug resistance eventually develops in most cases.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Most types of solid tumors harbor multiple mutations in cancer genes.
source: Most types of solid tumors harbor multiple, sometimes dozens of mutations, in cancer genes to establish the hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Vogelstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 41% of ccRCC tumors have inactivating mutations in the PBRM1 gene.
source: Varela et al. reported that 41% of ccRCC tumors had inactivating mutations in the PBRM1 gene.
evidence: This is supported by reference to a specific study by Varela et al.

claim: PBRM1 is a specificity subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex.
source: PBRM1 is a specificity subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex (Varela et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The high mutation rate of PBRM1 in ccRCC has been confirmed by multiple studies.
source: The high mutation rate of PBRM1 in ccRCC has been confirmed by multiple studies, together with mutations in other genes such as BAP1, SETD2, KDM5C/JARID1C, PTEN and UTX (Dalgliesh et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012; Peña-Llopis et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2013; Sato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The mutation rates of BAP1, SETD2, KDM5C/JARID1C, PTEN and UTX are much lower than that of PBRM1.
source: However, the mutation rates of the other genes are much lower than that of PBRM1 (Liao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PBRM1 mutations are predominantly inactivating in both alleles.
source: Its mutations are predominantly inactivating in both alleles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PBRM1 mutations.

claim: PBRM1 suppression causes changes in pathways regulating chromosome instability and cell proliferation.
source: PBRM1 suppression causes changes in pathways regulating chromosome instability and cell proliferation (Varela et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Many PBRM1 mutations occur early in tumorigenesis, like VHL mutations.
source: Like VHL mutations, many PBRM1 mutations occur early in tumorigenesis, unlike the other secondary mutations (Gerlinger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A PBRM1 germline mutation was reported to predispose patients to ccRCC.
source: Recently a PBRM1 germline mutation was reported to predispose patients to ccRCC (Benusiglio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PBRM1 was found to amplify a HIF signature.
source: PBRM1 was also found to amplify a HIF signature (Gao et al., 2017) and genetic ablation of both Vhl and Pbrm1 in mouse kidneys leads to ccRCC while single loss fails to do so (Nargund et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genetic ablation of both Vhl and Pbrm1 in mouse kidneys leads to ccRCC while single loss fails to do so.
source: PBRM1 was also found to amplify a HIF signature (Gao et al., 2017) and genetic ablation of both Vhl and Pbrm1 in mouse kidneys leads to ccRCC while single loss fails to do so (Nargund et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: KDM5C/JARID1C is a histone demethylase that removes methyl groups from tri-methylated lysine four on histone H3 (H3K4me3).
source: KDM5C/JARID1C is a histone demethylase that removes methyl groups from tri-methylated lysine four on histone H3 (H3K4me3).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KDM5C function.

claim: H3K4me3 is a histone mark that is tightly linked to actively transcribed genes.
source: H3K4me3 is a histone mark that is tightly linked to actively transcribed genes (Barski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: KDM5C mutations occur in 3-7% of ccRCC tumors.
source: KDM5C mutations occur in 3–7% of ccRCC tumors (Varela et al., 2011; Dalgliesh et al., 2010; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2013; Sato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: KDM5C mutations are mostly subclonal and happen later during tumor development.
source: Its mutations are mostly subclonal and happen later during tumor development (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Gerlinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HIF increases KDM5C levels and activity.
source: HIF increases KDM5C levels and activity, and the overall level of H3K4me3 is elevated when KDM5C is suppressed in VHL-defective kidney cancer cells (Niu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The overall level of H3K4me3 is elevated when KDM5C is suppressed in VHL-defective kidney cancer cells.
source: HIF increases KDM5C levels and activity, and the overall level of H3K4me3 is elevated when KDM5C is suppressed in VHL-defective kidney cancer cells (Niu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HIF-induced KDM5C is tumor-suppressive.
source: In addition, evidence suggests that HIF-induced KDM5C is tumor-suppressive, and this constitutes a negative feedback loop in regard to tumor growth (Niu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HIF-induced KDM5C constitutes a negative feedback loop in regard to tumor growth.
source: In addition, evidence suggests that HIF-induced KDM5C is tumor-suppressive, and this constitutes a negative feedback loop in regard to tumor growth (Niu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 is a histone-modifying enzyme that tri-methylates histone H3 at Lysine 36 (H3K36me3).
source: SETD2 is a histone-modifying enzyme that tri-methylates histone H3 at Lysine 36 (H3K36me3).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SETD2 function.

claim: SETD2 is mutated in 10-15% of ccRCC tumors.
source: It is mutated in 10 – 15% of ccRCC tumors (Dalgliesh et al., 2010; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2013; Sato et al., 2013; Hakimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: SETD2 is located on chromosome 3p like VHL and PBRM1.
source: It is also located on chromosome 3 p like VHL and PBRM1.
evidence: This is established genomic knowledge.

claim: SETD2 mutations are subclonal in ccRCC tumors.
source: SETD2 mutations are subclonalin ccRCC tumors (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Gerlinger et al., 2014; Sankin et al., 2014), and are associated with worse patient survival (Hakimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 mutations are associated with worse patient survival.
source: SETD2 mutations are subclonalin ccRCC tumors (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Gerlinger et al., 2014; Sankin et al., 2014), and are associated with worse patient survival (Hakimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 deficiency was reported to be associated with alternative splicing and transcriptional repression.
source: SETD2 deficiency was reported to be associated with alternative splicing and transcriptional repression (Wagner and Carpenter, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 mutations in ccRCC tumors are associated with changes in chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation.
source: Indeed, SETD2 mutations in ccRCC tumors are associated with changes in chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation (Buck et al., 2014) or widespread RNA processing defects (Simon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 mutations in ccRCC tumors are associated with widespread RNA processing defects.
source: Indeed, SETD2 mutations in ccRCC tumors are associated with changes in chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation (Buck et al., 2014) or widespread RNA processing defects (Simon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 regulates interferon signaling by methylating STAT1.
source: Recently, SETD2 was shown to regulate interferon signaling by methylating STAT1 (Chen et al., 2017), and to maintain mitosis and cytokinesis through methylating α-tubulin (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 maintains mitosis and cytokinesis through methylating α-tubulin.
source: Recently, SETD2 was shown to regulate interferon signaling by methylating STAT1 (Chen et al., 2017), and to maintain mitosis and cytokinesis through methylating α-tubulin (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BAP1 is a histone modifying enzyme.
source: Like KDM5C and SETD2, BAP1 is also a histone modifying enzyme.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BAP1 function.

claim: BAP1 is inactivated in 10-15% of ccRCC.
source: BAP1 is inactivated in 10 – 15% of ccRCC (Guo et al., 2012; Peña-Llopis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The BAP1 gene is located on chromosome 3 at band 3p21, which is very close to the PBRM1 gene.
source: The BAP1 gene is located on chromosome 3 at band 3p21, which is very close to the PBRM1 gene.
evidence: This is established genomic knowledge.

claim: Biallelic inactivation of BAP1 via mutation and loss of heterozygosity fits a two-hit tumor suppressor profile.
source: As with VHL, PBRM1 and SETD2, biallelic inactivation of BAP1 via mutation and loss of heterozygosity fit a two-hit tumor suppressor profile.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about BAP1 mutation patterns.

claim: Germline mutations of BAP1 predispose patients to ccRCC, uveal melanomas, mesothelioma, lung adenocarcinoma, meningioma, breast carcinoma and paraganglioma.
source: Germline mutations of BAP1 predispose patients to ccRCC, uveal melanomas, mesothelioma, lung adenocarcinoma, meningioma, breast carcinoma and paraganglioma (Abdel-Rahman et al., 2011; Wadt et al., 2012; Cheung et al., 2013; Pilarski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Loss of BAP1 is associated with worse patient survival in ccRCC.
source: Loss of BAP1 is associated with worse patient survival in ccRCC and seems to be mutually exclusive withPBRM1 mutations (Joseph et al., 2014; Joseph et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BAP1 loss seems to be mutually exclusive with PBRM1 mutations.
source: Loss of BAP1 is associated with worse patient survival in ccRCC and seems to be mutually exclusive withPBRM1 mutations (Joseph et al., 2014; Joseph et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BAP1 protein was reported to form a complex with host cell factor-1 (HCF-1) and promotes DNA double-strand break repair.
source: BAP1 protein was reported to form a complex with host cell factor-1 (HCF-1) and promotes DNA double-strand break repair (Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BAP1 forms a complex with ASXL1 which is essential for its ability to deubiquitinate histone H2A on lysine 119.
source: It also forms a complex with ASXL1 which is essential for its ability to deubiquitinate histone H2A on lysine 119, and this function regulates cell proliferation (Daou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BAP1's deubiquitination of histone H2A on lysine 119 regulates cell proliferation.
source: It also forms a complex with ASXL1 which is essential for its ability to deubiquitinate histone H2A on lysine 119, and this function regulates cell proliferation (Daou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BAP1 regulates IP3R3-mediated Ca2+ to mitochondria to suppress cell transformation.
source: Recently it was shown to regulate IP3R3-mediated Ca2+ to mitochondria to suppress cell transformation (Bononi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PBRM1 loss in VHL-/- cells elicited a higher number of transcriptional changes than in VHL+/+ cells.
source: PBRM1 loss in VHL-/- cells elicited a higher number of transcriptional changes than in VHL+/+ cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In VHL-/- cells, the transcriptional responses to PBRM1 depletion or VHL re-expression shared a group of gene targets.
source: In addition, in VHL-/- cells, the transcriptional responses to PBRM1 depletion or VHL re-expression shared a group of gene targets (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PBRM1 loss amplifies a HIF signature.
source: This is consistent with the previous observation that PBRM1 loss amplifies a HIF signature (Gao et al., 2017; Nargund et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Type I IFN signaling pathway and response to virus are commonly affected by genes shared between PBRM1 depletion and VHL re-expression.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) pathway analysis of the shared genes revealed that type I IFN signaling pathway and response to virus are commonly affected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by GO pathway analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expression signature of interferon alpha response was negatively correlated with PBRM1 suppression.
source: Gene Sets Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) confirmed that the expression signature of interferon alpha response was negatively correlated with PBRM1 suppression (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: KDM5C loss in VHL-/- cells elicited greater transcriptional changes than that in VHL+/+ cells.
source: Similar to PBRM1 suppression, KDM5C loss in VHL-/- cells elicited greater transcriptional changes than that in VHL+/+ cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In VHL-/- cells, transcriptional responses to KDM5C depletion or VHL re-expression shared a group of gene targets.
source: We also observed that in VHL-/- cells, transcriptional responses to KDM5C depletion or VHL re-expression shared a group of gene targets (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HIF activates KDM5C and this constitutes a negative feedback loop.
source: This is consistent with the previous observation that HIF activates KDM5C and this constitutes a negative feedback loop (Niu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The type I IFN signaling pathway, the expression signature of interferon alpha response, and the IFN-responsive genes were impacted by KDM5C loss.
source: GO pathway analysis, GSEA, and gene expression data confirmed that the type I IFN signaling pathway, the expression signature of interferon alpha response, and the IFN-responsive genes were impacted by KDM5C loss (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by GO pathway analysis, GSEA, and gene expression data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: The vast majority of the upregulated genes and downregulated genes after suppression of PBRM1 or KDM5C were shared.
source: The vast majority of the upregulated genes and downregulated genes after suppression of PBRM1 or KDM5C were shared (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Response to virus was significantly enriched among shared genes induced by PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression.
source: The GO pathway analysis of the shared genes that are suppressed by PBRM1 or KDM5C did not reveal any significantly impacted pathway, but the shared induced genes showed that "response to virus" was significantly enriched (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by GO pathway analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PBRM1 interacts with KDM5C.
source: When both proteins are expressed in HEK293T cells, immunoprecipitation of either protein pulled down the other (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Over-expressed Flag-PBRM1 was able to immunoprecipitate endogenous KDM5C protein and other PBAF subunits.
source: In addition, over-expressed Flag-PBRM1 was able to immunoprecipitate endogenous KDM5C protein and other PBAF subunits (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Flag-KDM5C was able to pull down endogenous PBRM1 along with BRG1 and BAF170.
source: Flag-KDM5C was able to pull down endogenous PBRM1 along with BRG1 and BAF170, the catalytic and structural subunits of PBAF complex respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Flag-KDM5C did not significantly co-IP BRD7 or BAF57.
source: Interestingly, it did not significantly co-IP BRD7 or BAF57, unlike that of Flag-PBRM1 (Figure 4B), suggesting that Flag-KDM5C pulled down a partial PBAF complex.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Flag-KDM5C pulled down a partial PBAF complex.
source: Interestingly, it did not significantly co-IP BRD7 or BAF57, unlike that of Flag-PBRM1 (Figure 4B), suggesting that Flag-KDM5C pulled down a partial PBAF complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential co-IP results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The endogenous PBRM1 pulled down the endogenous KDM5C in HEK293T cells along with the other PBAF subunits.
source: Moreover, the endogenous PBRM1 also pulled down the endogenous KDM5C in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells along with the other PBAF subunits (Figure 4D), suggesting that their interaction is not an artifact due to over-expression.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The interaction between PBRM1 and KDM5C is not an artifact due to over-expression.
source: Moreover, the endogenous PBRM1 also pulled down the endogenous KDM5C in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells along with the other PBAF subunits (Figure 4D), suggesting that their interaction is not an artifact due to over-expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the endogenous co-IP results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PBRM1's C-terminus, possibly the HMG domain, is important for KDM5C interaction.
source: PBRM1 truncation analysis suggested that its C-terminus, possibly the HMG domain, is important for KDM5C interaction (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by truncation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PBRM1 and KDM5C exist in one protein complex.
source: These results suggest that two proteins exist in one protein complex, and this could be the mechanism that they regulate the expression of similar target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: A group of 27 genes was suppressed by VHL but induced by PBRM1 or KDM5C.
source: Comparison of the transcriptional changes revealed that a group of 27 genes was suppressed by VHL but induced by PBRM1 or KDM5C (Figure 5A), and these genes were the interferon-responsive genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The 27 genes suppressed by VHL but induced by PBRM1 or KDM5C were interferon-responsive genes.
source: Comparison of the transcriptional changes revealed that a group of 27 genes was suppressed by VHL but induced by PBRM1 or KDM5C (Figure 5A), and these genes were the interferon-responsive genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The shared genes regulated by VHL, PBRM1 and KDM5C belong to the type I interferon signaling pathway.
source: A GO pathway analysis showed that these shared genes belong to the type I interferon signaling pathway (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by GO pathway analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After HIF2α suppression, the protein levels of IRF9 and STAT2 were reduced while the STAT1 protein level did not change in 786-O cells.
source: To test this, we suppressed HIF2α expression with two shRNA constructs in 786-O cells, then examined the expression of the ISGF3 components. After HIF2α suppression, the protein levels of IRF9 and STAT2 were reduced while the STAT1 protein level did not change (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Transient expression of a stable and active form of HIF2α in VHL+/+ ccRCC cell lines slightly increased the expression levels of ISGF3 and its targets.
source: Conversely, transient expression of a stable and active form of HIF2α in VHL+/+ccRCC cell lines, Caki-1 and Ren-01, slightly increased the expression levels of ISGF3 and its targets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Suppression of HIF1α did not reduce ISGF3 protein level or function in RCC4 cells.
source: Suppression of HIF1α did not reduce ISGF3 protein level or function in RCC4 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In PBRM1 knockdown 786-O cells, the protein levels of IRF9 and STAT2 were lower compared to control.
source: To test whether PBRM1 and KDM5C also had similar effects on ISGF3, we examined its components in 786-O cells with PBRM1 and KDM5C knocked down with various shRNA constructs. In PBRM1 knockdown cells, the protein levels of IRF9 and STAT2 were lower compared to control (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In KDM5C knockdown 786-O cells, the protein level of STAT2 was lower.
source: In KDM5C knockdown cells, the protein level of STAT2 was lower (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The expression of ISGF3 target genes were significantly reduced in 786-O cells after PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression.
source: Consistent with this, the expression of ISGF3 target genes were significantly reduced in 786-O cells after PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: After HIF2α suppression in Ren-02 cells, all three subunits of ISGF3 showed reduced expression.
source: To ensure that this observation is not confined to just one ccRCC cell line, we knocked down HIF2α, PBRM1 or KDM5C in another VHL-deficient ccRCC cell line, Ren-02. After HIF2α suppression, all three subunits of ISGF3 showed reduced expression (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: After PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression in Ren-02 cells, the protein levels of IRF9 and STAT2 dropped.
source: After PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression, the protein levels of IRF9 and STAT2 dropped (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The expression of ISGF3 target genes was significantly reduced in Ren-02 cells after PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression.
source: Consistent with this, the expression of ISGF3 target genes was significantly reduced in Ren-02 cells after PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: ISGF3 was mostly unphosphorylated in 786-O cells with or without PBRM1 or KDM5C knocked down.
source: ISGF3 can be activated by either interferon-induced phosphorylation on STAT1 and STAT2 or increased unphosphorylated protein levels (Cheon et al., 2013; Borden et al., 2007). To determine the phosphorylation status of ISGF3, we used interferon α to stimulate 786-O cells with or without PBRM1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A) or KDM5C (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B) knocked down and found that the ISGF3 was mostly unphosphorylated.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claim: The elevated protein levels of ISGF3 components are responsible for the enhanced activity of ISGF3.
source: This suggests that the elevated protein levels of ISGF3 components are responsible for the enhanced activity of ISGF3.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ISGF3 is mostly unphosphorylated.

claim: SETD2 promotes ISGF3 activity through methylating STAT1 after interferon stimulation.
source: A recent report suggested that SETD2 promotes ISGF3 activity through methylating STAT1 after interferon stimulation (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Knockdown of SETD2 in Ren-02 cells led to significant down-regulation of IRF9 and STAT2.
source: We knocked down the expression of SETD2 and BAP1 with shRNA constructs in Ren-02 cells and observed significant down-regulation of IRF9 and STAT2 (Figure 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of BAP1 in Ren-02 cells led to significant down-regulation of IRF9 and STAT2.
source: We knocked down the expression of SETD2 and BAP1 with shRNA constructs in Ren-02 cells and observed significant down-regulation of IRF9 and STAT2 (Figure 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of SETD2 or BAP1 in Ren-02 cells led to reduced expression of PLSCR1 and MX1.
source: In addition, we observed reduced expression of PLSCR1 and MX1, two ISGF3 targets.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: BAP1 re-expression in a Ren-02 BAP1 knockdown or knockout clone increased the protein levels of STAT2, IRF9 and PLSCR1.
source: BAP1 re-expression in a Ren-02 BAP1 knockdown (Figure 6B, left) or knockout clone (Figure 6B, right) generated by CRISPR/Cas9 increased the protein levels of STAT2, IRF9 and PLSCR1, suggesting that BAP1's impact on ISGF3 is specific.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: BAP1's impact on ISGF3 is specific.
source: BAP1 re-expression in a Ren-02 BAP1 knockdown (Figure 6B, left) or knockout clone (Figure 6B, right) generated by CRISPR/Cas9 increased the protein levels of STAT2, IRF9 and PLSCR1, suggesting that BAP1's impact on ISGF3 is specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Suppression of BAP1 in RCC4 cells led to reduced expression of IRF9, STAT2, PLSCR1 and MX1.
source: To ensure that this effect is not confined to one cell line, we knocked down the expression of BAP1 or SETD2 in RCC4 and BAP1 in A498 cells (A498 has an inactivating mutation in SETD2 so it is not suitable for SETD2 analysis), two additional VHL-deficient ccRCC cell lines. Their suppression also led to the reduced expression of IRF9, STAT2, PLSCR1 and MX1 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Suppression of SETD2 in RCC4 cells led to reduced expression of IRF9, STAT2, PLSCR1 and MX1.
source: To ensure that this effect is not confined to one cell line, we knocked down the expression of BAP1 or SETD2 in RCC4 and BAP1 in A498 cells (A498 has an inactivating mutation in SETD2 so it is not suitable for SETD2 analysis), two additional VHL-deficient ccRCC cell lines. Their suppression also led to the reduced expression of IRF9, STAT2, PLSCR1 and MX1 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Suppression of BAP1 in A498 cells led to reduced expression of IRF9, STAT2, PLSCR1 and MX1.
source: To ensure that this effect is not confined to one cell line, we knocked down the expression of BAP1 or SETD2 in RCC4 and BAP1 in A498 cells (A498 has an inactivating mutation in SETD2 so it is not suitable for SETD2 analysis), two additional VHL-deficient ccRCC cell lines. Their suppression also led to the reduced expression of IRF9, STAT2, PLSCR1 and MX1 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The impact of BAP1 loss in A498 cells was reversed by BAP1 re-expression.
source: Again, the impact of BAP1 loss in A498 cells was reversed by BAP1 re-expression (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expression of wild type or N78S BAP1 increased ISGF3 protein levels and its activity in UMRC2 and UMRC6 cells.
source: In order to further examine the impact of BAP1 on ISGF3 expression and activity, we expressed GFP, wild type BAP1, or BAP1 with tumor-derived mutations (N78S or G185R) in BAP1 null ccRCC cell lines UMRC2 and UMRC6. Expression of wild type or N78S BAP1 clearly increased ISGF3 protein levels and its activity in these cells, while the G185R mutant failed to do so (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: The G185R BAP1 mutant failed to increase ISGF3 protein levels and its activity in UMRC2 and UMRC6 cells.
source: In order to further examine the impact of BAP1 on ISGF3 expression and activity, we expressed GFP, wild type BAP1, or BAP1 with tumor-derived mutations (N78S or G185R) in BAP1 null ccRCC cell lines UMRC2 and UMRC6. Expression of wild type or N78S BAP1 clearly increased ISGF3 protein levels and its activity in these cells, while the G185R mutant failed to do so (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: SETD2 and BAP1 are required to maintain the expression and function of ISGF3 in multiple VHL-deficient ccRCC cell lines.
source: Thus SETD2 and BAP1 also are required to maintain the expression and function of ISGF3 in multiple VHL-deficient ccRCC cell lines.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that loss of SETD2 or BAP1 reduces ISGF3 levels and activity.

claim: A ccRCC tumor-derived mutation in BAP1 (G185R) disrupted its function in regulating ISGF3 in BAP1-null cells.
source: As a ccRCC tumor-derived mutation in BAP1 disrupted this function in both BAP1-null cells, it suggests that the regulation of ISGF3 is important to BAP1's tumor suppressor function.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that the G185R mutant failed to rescue ISGF3 levels.

claim: The regulation of ISGF3 is important to BAP1's tumor suppressor function.
source: As a ccRCC tumor-derived mutation in BAP1 disrupted this function in both BAP1-null cells, it suggests that the regulation of ISGF3 is important to BAP1's tumor suppressor function.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that a tumor-derived BAP1 mutation disrupts ISGF3 regulation.

claim: Suppression of IRF9 did not significantly change cell growth in culture.
source: Suppression of IRF9 did not significantly change cell growth in culture (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by cell growth assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 786-O cells with IRF9 suppression produced much larger tumors than the control cells in a xenograft model.
source: We injected the same number of 786-O cells expressing control shRNA (SCR) or IRF-sh69 into the flanks of nude mice. The 786-O cells with IRF9 suppression produced much larger tumors than the control cells (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by xenograft data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Knockdown of IRF9 in Ren-02 cells significantly boosted tumor growth in a xenograft model.
source: Knockdown of IRF9 in Ren-02 cells also significantly boosted tumor growth in a xenograft model (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: IRF9 suppression did not reduce the expression of other subunits of ISGF3.
source: IRF9 suppression did not reduce the expression of other subunits of ISGF3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: IRF9 suppression was maintained in the endpoint tumors.
source: and IRF9 suppression was maintained in the endpoint tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Suppression of STAT1 or STAT2 in 786-O cells led to significantly bigger tumors than control cells in a xenograft model.
source: Furthermore, we stably suppressed the expression of either STAT1 or STAT2 in 786-O cells then performed xenograft analysis. In both cases, the tumors were significantly bigger than the ones made by the control cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: ISGF3 has potent anti-tumor activity in vivo.
source: These data strongly suggest that ISGF3 has potent anti-tumor activity in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft data showing that loss of ISGF3 components enhances tumor growth.

claim: Control tumors contained higher percentages of mouse stromal cells, while the IRF9 knockdown tumors were mostly comprised of cancer cells.
source: The control tumors contained higher percentages of mouse stromal cells, while the IRF9 knockdown tumors were mostly comprised of cancer cells (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by H&E and IHC data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The cancer cells in tumors with IRF9 knockdown had a slight but insignificant increase in Ki67 staining over cancer cells in control tumors.
source: The cancer cells in tumors with IRF9 knockdown had a slight but insignificant increase in Ki67 staining, a marker for cell proliferation, over cancer cells in control tumors (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: CD45 staining was significantly higher in control tumors compared to IRF9 knockdown tumors.
source: However, CD45 staining, a marker for all mouse immune cells, was significantly higher in control tumors compared to IRF9 knockdown tumors (Figure 7E, p=0.007).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: There were no significant differences in cleaved caspase three or CD31 between control and IRF9 knockdown tumors.
source: There were no significant differences in cleaved caspase three or CD31, markers for apoptosis or blood vessels, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The lack of infiltrating host immune cells into the tumors formed by ccRCC cells depleted of IRF9 might be the primary reason of enhanced growth.
source: Thus the lack of infiltrating host immune cells into the tumors formed by ccRCC cells depleted of IRF9, not changes in cell proliferation, apoptosis, or blood vessel growth, might be the primary reason of enhanced growth.
evidence: This is speculated based on the IHC data showing reduced immune cell infiltration.

claim: Over-expression of STAT2 + IRF9 strongly induced ISGF3 targets PLSCR1 and MX1 in 786-O PBRM1-sh94 cells.
source: To this end, we stably infected 786-O PBRM1-sh94 cells with different combinations of viral vectors expressing STAT1, STAT2 or IRF9. The combination of STAT2 +IRF9 or all three factors strongly induced ISGF3 targets PLSCR1 and MX1 (Figure 8A) and we chose the cells expressing STAT2 +IRF9 for further analysis.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Over-expression of STAT2 + IRF9 did not change cell growth in culture.
source: The over-expression of STAT2 +IRF9 did not change cell growth in culture (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is supported by cell growth assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Overexpression of STAT2 + IRF9 strongly suppressed tumor growth by PBRM1-deficient 786-O cells in a xenograft model.
source: however, overexpression of these ISGF3 components strongly suppressed tumor growth by PBRM1-deficient 786-O cells in a xenograft model (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by xenograft data shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: Depletion of ISGF3 greatly enhanced tumor growth while its activation very potently blocked it.
source: Thus depletion of ISGF3 greatly enhanced tumor growth while its activation very potently blocked it, suggesting that ISGF3 is a central player in ccRCC tumor growth that is targeted by most of the cancer genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft data showing opposite effects of ISGF3 loss and gain.

claim: ISGF3 is a central player in ccRCC tumor growth that is targeted by most of the cancer genes.
source: Thus depletion of ISGF3 greatly enhanced tumor growth while its activation very potently blocked it, suggesting that ISGF3 is a central player in ccRCC tumor growth that is targeted by most of the cancer genes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that multiple tumor suppressors converge on ISGF3.

claim: Nuclear IRF9 and cytoplasmic STAT2 both significantly correlated with the expression of PBRM1, SETD2, or BAP1 in ccRCC TMA.
source: After scoring the samples and performing statistical analysis, the Spearman association analysis revealed that nuclear IRF9 and cytoplasmic STAT2 both significantly correlated with the expression of PBRM1, SETD2, or BAP1 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The loss of nuclear staining of IRF9 was associated with worse patient survival.
source: Interestingly, the loss of nuclear staining of IRF9 was associated with worse patient survival, consistent with a tumor suppressor role of ISGF3 (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The loss of cytoplasmic STAT2 staining was not associated with worse patient survival.
source: The loss of cytoplasmic STAT2 staining was not associated with worse patient survival (Figure 9D), suggesting that other ISGF3 components are the more dominant players in the human ccRCC.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Other ISGF3 components are the more dominant players in human ccRCC than STAT2.
source: The loss of cytoplasmic STAT2 staining was not associated with worse patient survival (Figure 9D), suggesting that other ISGF3 components are the more dominant players in the human ccRCC.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential survival associations of IRF9 and STAT2.

claim: The links between PBRM1, SETD2 or BAP1 and ISGF3 are preserved in human ccRCC tumors.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that the links between PBRM1, SETD2 or BAP1 and ISGF3 are preserved in human ccRCC tumors.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis in the TMA.

claim: HIF activates ISGF3 that suppresses tumor growth.
source: HIF activates ISGF3 that suppresses tumor growth. PBRM1, KDM5C, SETD2 and BAP1 all support the function of ISGF3.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 9E.

claim: PBRM1, KDM5C, SETD2 and BAP1 all support the function of ISGF3.
source: HIF activates ISGF3 that suppresses tumor growth. PBRM1, KDM5C, SETD2 and BAP1 all support the function of ISGF3.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 9E.

claim: Mutations in PBRM1, KDM5C, SETD2 or BAP1 relieve the tumor suppressive function of HIF2α.
source: Mutations in any of them relieve the tumor suppressive function of HIF2α.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 9E.

claim: Vhl conditional knockout in mouse kidneys alone is not sufficient to generate ccRCC despite fully activated HIF.
source: Consistent with this, Vhl conditional knockout in mouse kidneys alone is not sufficient to generate ccRCC despite fully activated HIF.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Only after combination with Pbrm1 or Bap1 conditional knockout can Vhl loss lead to kidney tumors.
source: Only after combination with Pbrm1 or Bap1 conditional knockout can Vhl loss lead to kidney tumors (Nargund et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HIF activates ISGF3, which constitutes a negative feedback loop in ccRCC.
source: Thus HIF could activate ISGF3, which constitutes a negative feedback loop in ccRCC.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental findings.

claim: ISGF3's inhibitory effect on tumor growth can be relieved by the loss of PBRM1, KDM5C, SETD2 or BAP1 to promote robust tumor growth.
source: Its inhibitory effect on tumor growth can be relieved by the loss of PBRM1, KDM5C, SETD2 or BAP1 to promote robust tumor growth (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 9E.

claim: ISGF3 is traditionally activated by interferon stimulation through phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2.
source: ISGF3 is traditionally activated by interferon stimulation through phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2 (Borden et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Days after the initial activation, the posttranslational modifications disappear, yet ISGF3 can still maintain its activity as unphosphorylated ISGF3 (U-ISGF3) with greatly enhanced protein levels.
source: However, days after the initial activation, the posttranslational modifications (PTMs) disappear, yet ISGF3 can still maintain its activity as unphosphorylated ISGF3 (U-ISGF3) with greatly enhanced protein levels (Cheon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: U-ISGF3 activates fewer targets than phosphorylated ISGF3, but it still potently antagonizes viral infection and DNA damage.
source: U-ISGF3 activates fewer targets than phosphorylated ISGF3, but it still potently antagonizes viral infection and DNA damage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about U-ISGF3 function.

claim: ISGF3 is a predictive biomarker for chemotherapy and radiation in breast cancer.
source: In oncology, ISGF3 is known to be a predictive biomarker for chemotherapy and radiation in breast cancer (Weichselbaum et al., 2008), and it is also associated with drug-resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ISGF3 is associated with drug-resistance to immune checkpoint blockade.
source: In oncology, ISGF3 is known to be a predictive biomarker for chemotherapy and radiation in breast cancer (Weichselbaum et al., 2008), and it is also associated with drug-resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The FDA has granted priority review for ipilimumab/nivolumab in intermediate and poor-risk mRCC.
source: The FDA has granted priority review for ipilimumab/nivolumab in intermediate and poor-risk mRCC (Abernathy, 2017), with RCC experts declaring this combination the new standard of care in the treatment of mRCC (Chustecka, 2017; Rini, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in PBRM1 confer clinical benefit to ccRCC patients treated with anti-PD-1 alone or in combination with anti-CTLA-4 therapies.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in PBRM1 were discovered to confer clinical benefit to ccRCC patients treated with anti-PD-1 alone or in combination with anti-CTLA-4 therapies (Miao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PBRM1 mutations enhance T-cell-mediated killing in a melanoma model.
source: In addition, PBRM1 mutations were found to enhance T-cell-mediated killing in an unbiased, high-throughput screen in a melanoma model (Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PBRM1 and BAP1 mutations are truncal (root change) in many cases while the mutations of SETD2 and KDM5C are subclonal.
source: The fact that PBRM1 mutations, but not those of BAP1, SETD2, and KDM5C, are a predictive biomarker for response to immunotherapy is likely because PBRM1 and BAP1 mutations are truncal (root change) in many cases while the mutations of the other two are subclonal (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Gerlinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ccRCC harbors rampant intra-tumoral heterogeneity.
source: ccRCC is known to harbor rampant intra-tumoral heterogeneity (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Gerlinger et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inactivating mutations in PBRM1, SETD2, KDM5C and BAP1 tend to be focal in the tumors.
source: Inactivating mutations in PBRM1, SETD2, KDM5C and BAP1 tend to be focal in the tumors, so therapies that are designed to exploit the weakness induced by mutation of an individual gene could be problematic since it cannot treat the remaining cancer cells free of that mutation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about mutation patterns in ccRCC.

claim: Pbrm1 loss in mice and PBRM1-/- vs PBRM1 re-expressed human A704 cells showed that PBRM1 deficiency was linked to the activation of the JAK/STAT3 pathway.
source: Pbrm1 loss in mice and PBRM1-/- vs PBRM1 re-expressed human A704 cells showed that PBRM1 deficiency was linked to the activation of the JAK/STAT3 pathway (Nargund et al., 2017; Miao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: STAT3 and ISGF3 are two different, often times opposing, pathways.
source: STAT3 and ISGF3 are two different, often times opposing, pathways: ISGF3 is activated by type I IFN (Cheon et al., 2013), while STAT3 is activated by the IL6 family, oncogenes, and growth factors (Heinrich et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ISGF3 is activated by type I IFN.
source: STAT3 and ISGF3 are two different, often times opposing, pathways: ISGF3 is activated by type I IFN (Cheon et al., 2013), while STAT3 is activated by the IL6 family, oncogenes, and growth factors (Heinrich et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: STAT3 is activated by the IL6 family, oncogenes, and growth factors.
source: STAT3 and ISGF3 are two different, often times opposing, pathways: ISGF3 is activated by type I IFN (Cheon et al., 2013), while STAT3 is activated by the IL6 family, oncogenes, and growth factors (Heinrich et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: STAT3 is often considered an oncogene.
source: STAT3 is often considered an oncogene (Yuan et al., 2016), while STAT1 is usually considered a TSG (Stephanou and Latchman, 2003), and thus they appear to play opposing biological roles in tumorigenesis (Avalle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: STAT1 is usually considered a tumor suppressor gene.
source: STAT3 is often considered an oncogene (Yuan et al., 2016), while STAT1 is usually considered a TSG (Stephanou and Latchman, 2003), and thus they appear to play opposing biological roles in tumorigenesis (Avalle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: STAT3 and STAT1 appear to play opposing biological roles in tumorigenesis.
source: STAT3 is often considered an oncogene (Yuan et al., 2016), while STAT1 is usually considered a TSG (Stephanou and Latchman, 2003), and thus they appear to play opposing biological roles in tumorigenesis (Avalle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss of STAT3 leads to prolonged activation of STAT1 in human T lymphoma cells or mouse cells.
source: In human T lymphoma cells or mouse cells, loss of STAT3 leads to prolonged activation of STAT1 (Regis et al., 2008; Costa-Pereira et al., 2002; Maritano et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: STAT3 negatively regulates the type I IFN signaling pathway by inhibiting expression of IRF7, IRF9, STAT1 in diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
source: In addition, STAT3 negatively regulates the type I IFN signaling pathway by inhibiting expression of IRF7, IRF9, STAT1 in diffuse large B cell lymphoma (Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SETD2 methylates STAT1 to promote ISGF3 function after IFN stimulation.
source: In a recent publication, SETD2 was shown to methylate STAT1 to promote ISGF3 function (Chen et al., 2017). However, this requirement of SETD2 is not observed unless IFN is added to activate ISGF3.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The requirement of SETD2 for ISGF3 function is not observed unless IFN is added to activate ISGF3.
source: In a recent publication, SETD2 was shown to methylate STAT1 to promote ISGF3 function (Chen et al., 2017). However, this requirement of SETD2 is not observed unless IFN is added to activate ISGF3.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the literature.

claim: HIF activation is sufficient to increase the protein levels of STAT2 and IRF9, thus activating U-ISGF3.
source: In our system, no exogenous IFN was present, and HIF activation seemed to be sufficient to increase the protein levels of STAT2 and IRF9, thus it might activate U-ISGF3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental observations.

claim: The mRNA levels of STAT1, STAT2 and IRF9 mirror that of the proteins in 786-O cells with or without PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression.
source: In 786-O cells with or without PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression, the mRNA levels of STAT1, STAT2 and IRF9 mirror that of the proteins (data not shown), suggesting that the regulation of U-ISFG3 occurred at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: The regulation of U-ISGF3 occurred at the transcriptional level.
source: In 786-O cells with or without PBRM1 or KDM5C suppression, the mRNA levels of STAT1, STAT2 and IRF9 mirror that of the proteins (data not shown), suggesting that the regulation of U-ISFG3 occurred at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mRNA and protein levels correlate.

claim: BAP1 loss reduced the protein levels of STAT2 and IRF9 independent of PBRM1 status.
source: Interestingly, BAP1 loss reduced the protein levels of STAT2 and IRF9 independent of PBRM1 status, since RCC4 cells express no endogenous PBRM1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Over-expression of IFN-β recruited macrophages which suppressed tumor growth and metastasis in nude mice.
source: The heightened U-ISGF3 may attract more innate immune cells such as macrophages and NK cells to attack the tumors and curb tumor growth, as a previous report showed that over-expression of IFN-β recruited macrophages which suppressed tumor growth and metastasis in nude mice (Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PBRM1 and KDM5C regulate ISGF3 subunits at transcriptional level.
source: With our current preliminary data we think that PBRM1 and KDM5C regulate ISGF3 subunits at transcriptional level, while SETD2 and BAP1 regulate ISGF3 at post-translational modification level.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental observations.

claim: SETD2 and BAP1 regulate ISGF3 at post-translational modification level.
source: With our current preliminary data we think that PBRM1 and KDM5C regulate ISGF3 subunits at transcriptional level, while SETD2 and BAP1 regulate ISGF3 at post-translational modification level.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental observations.

claim: KDM5C mutations were reported to occur in the cells with PBRM1 mutations.
source: KDM5C mutations were reported to occur in the cells with PBRM1 mutations (Hsieh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.
